title: America's new bargain hunt
body: Americans are getting choosier about how they spend their money, with new signs of a nationwide bargain hunt. Why it matters: Consumer spending has remained resilient, helping power eye-popping economic growth. But a closer look at spending patterns suggests that households are trading down, hunting for deals and second-guessing discretionary purchases. What they're saying: "Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend," Target CEO Michael Fiddelke said last week. Kohl's CFO Jill Timm said earlier this week that higher-income consumers are trading down to its stores, while middle-income shoppers are choosing its cheaper in-house brands. Customers bought more items per transaction but paid less per item, she said. Discount grocer Grocery Outlet saw signs for the first time last quarter of shoppers trading down from pricier products, particularly premium beef, CEO Jason Potter said. The big picture: Households this year have faced a fresh erosion of purchasing power after years of adjusting to a higher cost of living. That makes sustaining the same level of consumption increasingly dependent on finding cheaper alternatives. The hunt for cheaper alternatives may help explain why Americans are still spending at a healthy clip even as their frustration with prices deepens. By the numbers: Americans' spending is tilted toward cheaper retailers more than at any point since 2021, according to the latest Bank of America Institute analysis of its customers' card spending and deposit account data. It "suggests consumers are becoming more price sensitive," BofA economists wrote. "While households continue to spend, they are increasingly seeking discounts as concerns about higher prices persist." The bank says travel is the exception, with spending shifting toward pricier options. (Though it warns that may reflect some Americans forgoing trips altogether — leaving wealthier travelers to account for a greater share of spending.) Zoom in: Separate card spending data from Navy Federal Credit Union shows Americans across income groups are shifting toward discount grocers and warehouse stores and spending less at restaurants. Households are spending $167 more per month on housing, household bills and gasoline than they did in the same period a year ago — leaving less room in their budgets for other purchases. What to watch: Nearly three-quarters of holiday shoppers are holding off on purchases until Black Friday or Cyber Monday in hopes of better deals, according to Deloitte. A record share plan to shop during the promotional period, yet expected spending ($624 on average) is unchanged from last year. The bottom line: U.S. consumers' ability to keep spending may depend on how much further they can stretch each dollar.
